items.title: $AG Big Tech Is Coming for Mining, and the Numbers Are Staggering. CNBC highlighted a Financial Times report that Anglo American is seeing “
items.content_excerpt: $AG Big Tech Is Coming for Mining, and the Numbers Are Staggering. CNBC highlighted a Financial Times report that Anglo American is seeing “deep interest” from major technology companies in mining investments. Amazon and Microsoft have reportedly expressed interest in securing physical uranium from Cameco, while BHP’s CFO has acknowledged discussions with hyperscalers. Now consider the bigger picture. The ENTIRE publicly traded global mining sector has an estimated combined market capitalization of approximately $2 trillion to $4 trillion. Meanwhile, just a handful of technology companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, collectively have market capitalizations many times greater. Think about that for a moment. These companies are spending hundreds of billions building AI infrastructure, data centers and the energy systems required to power them. Yet the entire publicly traded mining industry responsible for supplying many of the essential raw materials represents a fraction of their combined equity valuations. For a hyperscaler, investing $100 million, $1 Billion in a strategically important mining project could be relatively insignificant. For a miner, that same investment could be transformational. And if technology companies collectively directed even $100 billion toward mining investments and strategic supply agreements, that would represent approximately 3% of the entire publicly traded mining sector’s estimated market capitalization. Now consider silver. Silver is essential for electrical conductivity, solar technology, electronics and numerous advanced industrial applications. Unlike copper, silver is also a precious metal with monetary and investment demand. Furthermore, much of the world’s silver is produced as a byproduct of mining other metals, making supply relatively difficult to increase quickly in response to higher prices. That is where companies like First Majestic Silver ($AG) become particularly interesting. First Majestic offers substantial exposure to primary silver production at a time when industrial demand, investment demand and strategic interest in securing mineral supplies could increasingly converge. I’m not suggesting that $MSFT or $AMZN is about to acquire a silver miner, $TSLA / $SPCX might though. But I do believe we’re witnessing the early stages of a structural shift in how major corporations think about access to physical resources. For decades, technology companies have commanded enormous valuations while the mining industry has frequently struggled to attract sufficient development capital. What happens if even a relatively small portion of that technology-sector capital begins flowing upstream? Mining companies could gain access to entirely new sources of financing, strategic partnerships and long-term supply agreements. And investors may begin assigning greater value to established production, permitted assets and mineral resources in secure jurisdictions. Silver could benefit from this broader reassessment, even if the initial focus remains on copper, uranium and other critical minerals. I believe the next decade could fundamentally change how the market values companies controlling strategically important physical resources. And First Majestic is positioned to participate in that opportunity.

items.title: $AG Big Tech Is Coming for Mining, and the Numbers Are Staggering. CNBC highlighted a Financial Times report that Anglo American is seeing “
items.content_excerpt: $AG Big Tech Is Coming for Mining, and the Numbers Are Staggering. CNBC highlighted a Financial Times report that Anglo American is seeing “deep interest” from major technology companies in mining investments. Amazon and Microsoft have reportedly expressed interest in securing physical uranium from Cameco, while BHP’s CFO has acknowledged discussions with hyperscalers. Now consider the bigger picture. The ENTIRE publicly traded global mining sector has an estimated combined market capitalization of approximately $2 trillion to $4 trillion. Meanwhile, just a handful of technology companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, collectively have market capitalizations many times greater. Think about that for a moment. These companies are spending hundreds of billions building AI infrastructure, data centers and the energy systems required to power them. Yet the entire publicly traded mining industry responsible for supplying many of the essential raw materials represents a fraction of their combined equity valuations. For a hyperscaler, investing $100 million, $1 Billion in a strategically important mining project could be relatively insignificant. For a miner, that same investment could be transformational. And if technology companies collectively directed even $100 billion toward mining investments and strategic supply agreements, that would represent approximately 3% of the entire publicly traded mining sector’s estimated market capitalization. Now consider silver. Silver is essential for electrical conductivity, solar technology, electronics and numerous advanced industrial applications. Unlike copper, silver is also a precious metal with monetary and investment demand. Furthermore, much of the world’s silver is produced as a byproduct of mining other metals, making supply relatively difficult to increase quickly in response to higher prices. That is where companies like First Majestic Silver ($AG) become particularly interesting. First Majestic offers substantial exposure to primary silver production at a time when industrial demand, investment demand and strategic interest in securing mineral supplies could increasingly converge. I’m not suggesting that $MSFT or $AMZN is about to acquire a silver miner, $TSLA / $SPCX might though. But I do believe we’re witnessing the early stages of a structural shift in how major corporations think about access to physical resources. For decades, technology companies have commanded enormous valuations while the mining industry has frequently struggled to attract sufficient development capital. What happens if even a relatively small portion of that technology-sector capital begins flowing upstream? Mining companies could gain access to entirely new sources of financing, strategic partnerships and long-term supply agreements. And investors may begin assigning greater value to established production, permitted assets and mineral resources in secure jurisdictions. Silver could benefit from this broader reassessment, even if the initial focus remains on copper, uranium and other critical minerals. I believe the next decade could fundamentally change how the market values companies controlling strategically important physical resources. And First Majestic is positioned to participate in that opportunity.

items.content_excerpt: $APLD $WULF it is astonishing to me. Some $APLD bear said $WULF has “better margins.” WTF? “Better margins”? $APLD just reported roughly 89% HPC property-level NOI margins. $WULF targets 85%. Actual results versus a target is not evidence that WULF has superior margins. Indeed the evidence is the contrary. $APLD has 1,410 MW leased versus $WULF’s disclosed 839 MW (68% more) plus approximately $36 Billion base-term contracted revenue and 250 MW already operating. That’s a much larger contracted business for $APLD Anthropic is a great win for $WULF, but APLD counts $META and $ORCL as its tenants. And WULF passes electricity costs through to tenants, so cheaper power doesn’t automatically translate into higher landlord profits. Less debt alone doesn’t settle which stock deserves a premium. You have to weigh it against the business being financed. I favor $APLD much larger contracted portfolio, strong operating margins and demonstrated execution. And $WULF is trading on dangerous ground by risking everything by developing in anti-data center states like New York and Pennsylvania. $WULF does not deserve the higher valuation. $APLD does

items.title: Oct 15 Market Recap Not a crash, but instead a rotation happened today. $SPY was +0.33%, but the Dow led the way with +1.08% as money flowed
items.content_excerpt: Oct 15 Market Recap Not a crash, but instead a rotation happened today. $SPY was +0.33%, but the Dow led the way with +1.08% as money flowed into health care, retail, & rate-sensitive stocks. $QQQ finished slightly under -0.05% where chips sold off for a 2nd day after a hot CPI report on Wednesday & then an even hotter PPI report today at +1.3% in September, the biggest jump since March 2022! The problem with this is that more inflation means higher odds for the Feds to hike rates, & AI stocks that rely on borrowing feel that first. $TSM beat earnings but sounded cautious on 2027, adding to chip pressure. $IWM gained +1.38% as small caps caught the rotation and the 10-year yield dropped to 5.10%. $NKE was a top Dow performer, up 5%+, as beaten-down retail bounced. Other notable mentions, Neoclouds were down more than 10% but Coreweave ended up in green with the help of NVIDIA’s Jansen. Will tomorrow be a bounce back for tech?

items.title: $MU $QQQ $SKHY $PY Or not. Since this chip will not ship to any customer for several years and certainly not until after Samsung brings thei
items.content_excerpt: $MU $QQQ $SKHY $PY Or not. Since this chip will not ship to any customer for several years and certainly not until after Samsung brings theirs to market it sure seems like a non issue. This chip has not gone to customers for qualification and testing because it hasnt left the lab. It hasnt produced test samples. It has no fab. It has no purchase orders. Is this chip gonna be great? Probably, but It will never be exported out of China. People act like these high end memory chips grow on trees or that they take 10 seconds to stamp in a mold. They do not. They wouldnt be allowed to export something they have to import to be competitive until they can fill Chinese demand. That is a big ask considering CXMT is several years out to produce enough lpddr6 to meet Xaiomi demand, SK still meets 99% of that demand, contractually. CXMT cant and wont meet HBM3 demand for another 5 years, this CXMT's words, not mine. BS videos will get you nowhere.

A lot of background music regarding safety measures within the industry as well as higher capital costs. I believe that most of our debt is already agreed upon at favorable rates, and the chart will bear out that these sudden gaps down quickly recover once sanity prevails. I always measure my position by two things: was my original thesis about AI correct and has anything occurred that would negate that thesis. The fact that they are even comparing the AI build-out to the http://dot.com era tells me that most analysts in this sector do not know what they’re talking about. AI is not going anywhere. When I was younger, human beings answered the phone and customer service was exactly that. The push to profitability unfortunately excludes humans. Labor is generally the highest cost on the balance sheet. The chart shows oversold condition. Historically, NCIS has held the 200 day very well.

items.content_excerpt: Big pharmaceutical stocks are trading at or near all-time highs as investors shift away from volatile technology shares and seek more defensive investments amid the ongoing tech selloff. AbbVie, Eli Lilly and Gilead Sciences are attracting demand thanks to their diversified businesses, relatively predictable performance and continued investment in future drug pipelines. These companies are also working to extend patent protection for their best-selling medicines, helping sustain revenue and support long-term growth. Thursday’s gains reflected the sector’s strength: Eli Lilly rose 4.78%, AbbVie gained 1.13% and Gilead Sciences advanced 3.29%. Amgen climbed 3.03% and UnitedHealth Group increased 3.71%, while the healthcare sector ETF XLV gained 2.28% and the biotech ETF XBI rose 1.89%. Merck was a notable exception, slipping 0.21%. The rally highlights a broader rotation toward healthcare as investors look for stability amid technology-market turbulence. $LLY $ABBV $GILD $UNH $MRK

$AG Big Tech Is Coming for Mining, and the Numbers Are Staggering. CNBC highlighted a Financial Times report that Anglo American is seeing “deep interest” from major technology companies in mining investments. Amazon and Microsoft have reportedly expressed interest in securing physical uranium from Cameco, while BHP’s CFO has acknowledged discussions with hyperscalers. Now consider the bigger picture. The ENTIRE publicly traded global mining sector has an estimated combined market capitalization of approximately $2 trillion to $4 trillion. Meanwhile, just a handful of technology companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, collectively have market capitalizations many times greater. Think about that for a moment. These companies are spending hundreds of billions building AI infrastructure, data centers and the energy systems required to power them. Yet the entire publicly traded mining industry responsible for supplying many of the essential raw materials represents a fraction of their combined equity valuations. For a hyperscaler, investing $100 million, $1 Billion in a strategically important mining project could be relatively insignificant. For a miner, that same investment could be transformational. And if technology companies collectively directed even $100 billion toward mining investments and strategic supply agreements, that would represent approximately 3% of the entire publicly traded mining sector’s estimated market capitalization. Now consider silver. Silver is essential for electrical conductivity, solar technology, electronics and numerous advanced industrial applications. Unlike copper, silver is also a precious metal with monetary and investment demand. Furthermore, much of the world’s silver is produced as a byproduct of mining other metals, making supply relatively difficult to increase quickly in response to higher prices. That is where companies like First Majestic Silver ($AG) become particularly interesting. First Majestic offers substantial exposure to primary silver production at a time when industrial demand, investment demand and strategic interest in securing mineral supplies could increasingly converge. I’m not suggesting that $MSFT or $AMZN is about to acquire a silver miner, $TSLA / $SPCX might though. But I do believe we’re witnessing the early stages of a structural shift in how major corporations think about access to physical resources. For decades, technology companies have commanded enormous valuations while the mining industry has frequently struggled to attract sufficient development capital. What happens if even a relatively small portion of that technology-sector capital begins flowing upstream? Mining companies could gain access to entirely new sources of financing, strategic partnerships and long-term supply agreements. And investors may begin assigning greater value to established production, permitted assets and mineral resources in secure jurisdictions. Silver could benefit from this broader reassessment, even if the initial focus remains on copper, uranium and other critical minerals. I believe the next decade could fundamentally change how the market values companies controlling strategically important physical resources. And First Majestic is positioned to participate in that opportunity.
